screens.title: Structured Troubleshooting: Scientific Method
screens.narratorSegment: The scientific method gives you a disciplined way to reduce uncertainty in complex incidents. Start by observing: gather symptom data such as service error messages, metrics spikes, or user reports. From those observations form a hypothesis — a concise, testable claim like "the web server is slow because the database is overloaded." Next predict what you should see if that hypothesis is true, for example increased database C P U and slow query times. Then test your prediction with focused tools: run queries, check iostat, use ss or tcpdump, and inspect journalctl entries for correlated timestamps. Analyze the results: if evidence supports the hypothesis, implement a controlled fix and verify system behavior; if not, iterate with a refined hypothesis. A common mistake is skipping evidence collection before changing configuration; that destroys the ability to reproduce or analyze. Another pitfall is testing too many variables at once. A good concrete example: if users report timeouts, hypothesize whether network, app, or storage is causing latency, then predict measurable indicators for each and test them sequentially. The core takeaway is that a tested hypothesis is more reliable than guesswork and produces artifacts you can review later.

keyIdea.title: Testable Hypotheses Win
keyIdea.text: Turn observations into predictions and design focused tests; avoid making simultaneous changes that erase evidence.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.6 › Scientific Method
Process Steps
1. Observe
Collect errors, metrics, and user reports. Timestamped evidence is essential.
2. Hypothesize
Write a concise, testable cause such as resource exhaustion or a misconfiguration.
3. Predict & Test
Define what you expect to see and run focused commands to confirm or refute.
4. Analyze & Iterate
Interpret outputs, accept or refute the hypothesis, and repeat until resolved.
Key Takeaway

Design small, falsifiable tests and preserve artifacts before applying changes.

Concrete Example
Users report intermittent web timeouts. Hypothesis: database saturation. Prediction: database CPU and slow queries correlate with web timeouts. Test: sample iostat, database process CPU, and journalctl -u httpd with matching timestamps. If data matches, throttle or tune DB connections; if not, form a new hypothesis such as network packet loss and run ping/mtr and tcpdump next.
Common Mistake
Changing multiple settings at once and then claiming success without reproducible evidence.
Check Your Understanding
  • Can you state a testable hypothesis for a timeout issue?
  • What artifacts would you collect before making changes?

screens.title: Divide and Conquer Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: Divide and conquer is a complementary strategy that helps you quickly eliminate whole classes of causes. When a service is unreachable or slow, start by asking which broad domain could explain the symptoms: network, storage, or application. For example, if a service port is inaccessible, test basic connectivity first with ping and tcpdump to rule out network faults. If network checks pass, verify whether storage latency is causing slow responses with iostat or LVM tools. Only after isolating the domain should you dig into application-level logs with journalctl or strace. The value of this approach is that it prevents you from chasing irrelevant signals. A practical sequence might be: ping to verify host reachability, ss or netstat to confirm listening sockets, firewall checks with firewalld status or tcpdump to see dropped packets, then systemctl status and journalctl for the service itself. Remember that domains can interact: a network partition can cause application queues to fill, which then stresses storage. Document each boundary test so you can backtrack and combine evidence later. Divide and Conquer Troubleshooting means use simple boundary tests to rule out network, storage, or application layers before deep-diving into one area.. In practical terms, narrow the domain: network, storage, or application. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.6 › Divide & Conquer
Boundary Tests
Network: ping, mtr, ss, tcpdump to confirm reachability and packet flows.
Storage: iostat, LVM tools, and dmesg for I/O wait and disk errors.
Application: systemctl status, journalctl -u, strace for runtime failures.
Sequence Example
  1. Ping host and run ss to see if port is listening.
  2. If reachable, run tcpdump to check packet drops or firewall blocks.
  3. Inspect disk I/O and service logs if latency persists.
Analogy
Think of it like triage: you first check vital signs, then organ systems. Rapidly rule out whole domains so you can focus your technical work where it matters.
Example Walkthrough
Service unreachable. Ping succeeds but tcpdump shows RST packets; firewall logs indicate dropped packets. Conclusion: network firewall misconfiguration. If tcpdump had shown no packets at all, next step would be to check routing and network interfaces on the host and upstream switches.
Common Mistake
Assuming one domain in isolation when symptoms span multiple layers — always correlate timestamps across tools.
Key Takeaway

Systematically rule out domains using minimal tests to reduce your investigative surface quickly.

screens.title: sosreport — Collecting a Full Diagnostic Snapshot
screens.narratorSegment: sosreport packages a wide range of system information into a single compressed archive, which is extremely useful for support cases and baselining. You run it with sudo sosreport; it may prompt for a case ID and additional notes. The generated tar. xz contains configuration files, kernel modules, network and storage information, and system logs—everything a support engineer or an experienced troubleshooter needs to understand system state. Use sosreport when you need a complete snapshot before making large changes or when opening a support case. Handle the archive carefully because it can include sensitive data such as network configuration, installed packages, and log contents. A useful practice is to inspect contents locally before sharing and to redact or transfer the file using secure channels. content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.6 › sosreport
Definition & Purpose

sosreport gathers configuration, kernel and module data, networking and storage information, and logs into a single compressed archive for diagnostics or support cases. Use it to provide full context when targeted logs are insufficient.

Security Note
Because the archive may contain secrets or host-specific configuration, inspect and handle it using secure storage and transfer methods before sharing with support.
When to Run sosreport
  • Before large changes or upgrades.
  • When opening a support case with Red Hat.
  • To capture a baseline for comparison.
Run Example
sudo sosreport
# follow prompts; note the generated /var/tmp/xxxx-xxxx.tar.xz path
Inspect the archive before sharing and store it securely. Use the archive to accelerate support triage or to compare system states between working and failing hosts.
Key Takeaway

sosreport is a powerful evidence collector—use it when you need a full picture and always treat outputs as sensitive.

screens.title: kdump and vmcore — Capturing Kernel Panics
screens.narratorSegment: kdump is the kernel crash dumping facility that saves a memory image when the kernel panics. It reserves a portion of memory for a capture kernel; when the primary kernel fails, the machine boots a small capture kernel that writes the vmcore file to disk. That vmcore contains the system's memory image at the time of panic and is invaluable for diagnosing low-level kernel faults. To rely on kdump in production, ensure the kdump service is enabled and that you have reserved sufficient crashkernel memory in GRUB configuration, and that the dump target is a reliable storage path such as /var/crash or a network location. Testing kdump should be done only in VMs: you can trigger a panic with a safe, controlled command in a lab environment. After a reboot, verify that a vmcore file exists in /var/crash. One misconception is assuming vmcore analysis is trivial: it requires specialized tools like crash and kernel symbol knowledge. However, collecting the dump reliably is the critical first step and allows either your team or Red Hat to perform deeper analysis. kdump and vmcore — Capturing Kernel Panics means kdump preserves a vmcore image at panic time — configure, enable, and test kdump in vms so you have artifacts for kernel-level investigations.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.6 › kdump & vmcore
How kdump Works
kdump reserves memory for a capture kernel. On panic, the system boots into the capture kernel and writes a vmcore file containing the memory image. That vmcore is the primary artifact for kernel debugging.
Checks
  • sudo systemctl status kdump
  • Verify crashkernel parameter in GRUB
  • Confirm dump target exists and is writable
Safe Test (VM only)
# Only in VM lab
echo c | sudo tee /proc/sysrq-trigger
# system will reboot; after reboot check /var/crash/ for vmcore
vmcore Analysis
Analyzing vmcore typically requires the crash utility and kernel symbols. While analysis is specialized, simply capturing a reliable vmcore file is essential; it allows support engineers to pinpoint kernel stack traces, module involvement, and memory state at failure.
Common Mistake
Assuming a crash dump will be present after random reboots — verify kdump was enabled and that the dump target has space and correct permissions.
Key Takeaway

Configure and test kdump in a VM so kernel panics reliably produce vmcore artifacts for analysis.

screens.title: journalctl — Advanced Filtering and Queries
screens.narratorSegment: journalctl is the primary log analysis tool for systemd-based systems. While basic use shows you logs, advanced filtering transforms noisy output into targeted evidence. You can filter by unit with journalctl -u service, by priority using -p err or -p warning, by time range with --since and --until, and by executable using the _COMM field. Kernel messages are accessible via -k and you can follow live logs with -f. Combining filters is powerful: for example journalctl -u httpd. service --since "yesterday" -p err returns only error messages for the httpd unit since yesterday. Use -b -1 to review the previous boot if you suspect an issue that caused a reboot. A common misconception is relying only on text searches; timestamps and priority levels are often more reliable for correlation. Concrete example: when investigating a failing web service, filter journalctl by the unit and time window surrounding reported errors, then cross-reference those timestamps with network captures or iostat outputs. This focused approach quickly narrows the candidate causes and yields actionable log lines for further testing or support. journalctl — Advanced Filtering and Queries means use unit, priority, time, executable, and boot filters to find meaningful log entries fast before deep analysis.. In practical terms, reduce noise and surface relevant log entries quickly. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.6 › journalctl Filters
Filter Recipes
journalctl -u httpd.service --since "yesterday" -p err
journalctl _COMM=httpd --since "2 hours ago"
journalctl -k
journalctl -b -1
journalctl -u myservice -f
Combine unit, priority and time filters to locate relevant entries without scanning unrelated logs.
Practical Tip
Start broad, then add filters. Use -o short-iso for consistent timestamps you can correlate with other tools.
Example Scenario
If a service fails at 14:12, run journalctl -u <service> --since "14:00" --until "14:30" -p err to capture error lines and timestamps. Correlate those with tcpdump or iostat samples taken at the same period to identify cross-domain causes.
Misconception
Searching for text strings alone can miss context; always use time and priority filters to reduce false positives.
Key Takeaway

Use journalctl filters to narrow logs quickly, then correlate those results with other diagnostics for confident conclusions.

screens.title: Debugging systemd Units and Dependencies
screens.narratorSegment: systemd is central to how services are started and managed in RHEL. When a unit fails, begin with sudo systemctl status to see the current state and recent log lines. Use sudo systemctl is-failed to quickly check failure, and sudo systemctl show to inspect properties such as ExecStart, Environment, Requires, and resource limits. Display the unit file with sudo systemctl cat and verify ExecStart paths, user contexts, working directories, and file permissions. Also check dependencies with sudo systemctl list-dependencies to ensure required units are active. Common configuration issues include incorrect ExecStart paths, missing dependencies, and resource limits like LimitNOFILE or LimitNPROC that are too low. A practical workflow is: check status, fetch detailed logs with journalctl -u, inspect unit file content, verify environment and permissions, and then test the ExecStart command manually as the configured user. Misconceptions include assuming systemctl restart always fixes a misconfiguration; restarting frequently without addressing root causes can mask intermittent dependency or resource problems. Document your unit checks so you can reproduce fixes reliably. Debugging systemd Units and Dependencies means check unit status and properties first, then test the unit's execstart manually to reveal permission or path issues before changing service files.. In practical terms, find why services fail: status, properties, unit files, and resource limits. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Use sudo systemctl is-failed to quickly check failure, and sudo systemctl show to inspect properties such as ExecStart, Environment, Requires, and resource limits. Display the unit file with sudo systemctl cat and verify ExecStart paths, user contexts, working directories, and file permissions. Also check dependencies with sudo systemctl list-dependencies to ensure required units are active. Common configuration issues include incorrect ExecStart paths, missing dependencies, and resource limits like LimitNOFILE or LimitNPROC that are too low. A practical workflow is: check status, fetch detailed logs with journalctl -u, inspect unit file content, verify environment and permissions, and then test the ExecStart command manually as the configured user. Misconceptions include assuming systemctl restart always fixes a misconfiguration; restarting frequently without addressing root causes can mask intermittent dependency or resource problems. Document your unit checks so you can reproduce fixes reliably. Debugging systemd Units and Dependencies means check unit status and properties first, then test the unit's execstart manually to reveal permission or path issues before changing service files.. In practical terms, find why services fail: status, properties, unit files, and resource limits. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 2 › Chapter 1.6 › systemd Debugging
Essential Commands
sudo systemctl status <service>
sudo systemctl is-failed <service>
sudo systemctl show <service>
sudo systemctl list-dependencies <service>
sudo systemctl cat <service>
Use these commands to see runtime state, unit properties, dependency graphs, and the actual unit file contents for misconfigurations.
Common Issues
  • Wrong ExecStart path or missing script permissions
  • Missing required units not active at startup
  • Resource limits too restrictive causing process failure
Example Diagnosis
systemctl status shows failed ExecStart: No such file. Use systemctl cat to confirm the configured path, then run the command manually as the unit's user to reproduce the error. Fix the path or permissions and reload systemd, then restart and verify with journalctl -u.
Key Takeaway
Inspect unit files and properties first; manual execution of ExecStart often reveals permission and environment issues that systemd hides.

screens.title: Synthesize Multi-component Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: In real incidents you will often need to synthesize data from multiple components to form a convincing causal chain. Begin by assembling a timeline of events using timestamps from journalctl, application logs, monitoring metrics, and tcpdump captures. Create a sequence like: network error at T0, increased application retries at T1, elevated input and output wait at T2, system panic at T3. This timeline helps you reason about causality rather than correlation. Use sosreport to capture the overall environment and vmcore to capture kernel state if a panic occurred. When correlating data, pay attention to clock skew and timezone issues so timestamps align. One common pitfall is treating a symptom as the cause because it appears first in a log; instead, ask whether the observed symptom could be downstream of another failure. For practice, map out a hypothetical chain: firewall misconfiguration causing packet loss, which leads to application retry storms, increasing input and output, and eventually destabilizing the kernel. Document each test and decision so others can review and reproduce your analysis. Synthesize Multi-component Troubleshooting means correlate timestamps across logs and metrics to build a causal timeline. this turns scattered evidence into a coherent incident narrative.. In practical terms, combine evidence from network, app, storage, and kernel for complex incidents. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Forensic Timeline (Example)
T0: Network packets dropped (tcpdump)
T1: Application logs show increased retries (journalctl)
T2: I/O wait rises (iostat)
T3: Kernel panic and reboot; vmcore created by kdump
Assemble evidence with consistent timestamps and include recovered artifacts: tcpdump pcap, journalctl excerpts, iostat samples, sosreport archive, and vmcore if present.
Practical Advice
Keep a running incident log with exact commands you ran and the outputs you captured. This makes post-incident analysis and handoffs much more effective.
Misconception Check
Don't assume the first visible error is the root cause. Build the timeline to test causality and look for upstream triggers.

A careful timeline turns separate data points into an incident story you can act on and defend during a postmortem.

screens.title: Hands-on Scenario: Diagnose a Failing mywebapp.service
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on scenario walks through a realistic lab that you can reproduce in a VM. First, create a failing systemd unit that runs a script which accesses a non-existent file; enable and start it. Use sudo systemctl status mywebapp. service to see the failure and journalctl -u mywebapp. service --since "5 minutes ago" to read error lines. The likely error is No such file or directory for the ExecStart path. Correct the script or unit file, reload the daemon, and restart the service to verify successful execution. After fixing the unit, collect diagnostics with sudo sosreport and note the archive path for later analysis or support. Finally, verify kdump status and, only inside the VM, trigger a controlled kernel panic with the documented command to confirm that vmcore is saved to /var/crash. This sequence illustrates formulating a hypothesis, testing it, collecting a system snapshot, and validating kernel crash capture. A common trap is failing to collect sosreport before changes; preserve evidence first so you can compare before/after states. Did you document the commands and the archive path so the postmortem is reproducible?

keyIdea.title: Practice the Full Workflow
keyIdea.text: Simulate a failing unit, use systemctl and journalctl to diagnose, collect sosreport, and test kdump in a VM to validate end-to-end incident handling.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.6 › Lab Walkthrough
Starter Commands (Use in VM)
# Create failing script
sudo mkdir -p /opt/mywebapp
sudo tee /opt/mywebapp/run.sh <<EOF
#!/bin/bash
echo "Starting mywebapp..."
cat /non/existent/file
echo "mywebapp exited."
EOF
sudo chmod +x /opt/mywebapp/run.sh

# Create unit and start
sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/mywebapp.service <<EOF
[Unit]
Description=My Failing Web Application
After=network.target

[Service]
ExecStart=/opt/mywebapp/run.sh
Restart=on-failure

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
EOF

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now mywebapp.service
sudo systemctl status mywebapp.service
Diagnosis Steps
  • Check status and recent logs with systemctl and journalctl.
  • Fix the script to remove the failing cat command and re-run.
  • Collect sudo sosreport before further system changes.
kdump Check & VM Test
# Check kdump
sudo systemctl status kdump
# If enabled and VM ready, trigger panic (will reboot)
echo c | sudo tee /proc/sysrq-trigger
# After reboot, check /var/crash/ for vmcore
Only perform the panic test in a virtual lab. After verifying vmcore exists, include the crash dump and sosreport in your postmortem artifacts.
Key Takeaway

Work methodically: diagnose, fix, collect evidence, and test kernel capture in a VM to complete the workflow.

screens.title: Documenting and Communicating Findings
screens.narratorSegment: Documentation is an often overlooked but crucial part of troubleshooting. As you test hypotheses and gather evidence, keep a concise log of commands, timestamps, outputs, and the locations of any artifacts like sosreport archives or vmcore files. This runbook-style documentation does three things: it helps you reproduce the incident, it provides clear evidence for support engineers, and it forms the basis for a constructive postmortem. Use consistent timestamp formats when extracting logs so correlation across tools is straightforward. When handing off to a team or Red Hat support, include a short narrative: observed symptoms, hypotheses tested, commands executed, and a note of any configuration changes you made. A common misconception is assuming screenshots or ad-hoc notes are sufficient; structured logs and preserved artifacts are far more valuable. Finally, anonymize or redact sensitive data in any shared archives, and use secure transfer methods. Good documentation shortens resolution time in future incidents and helps your organization learn. Documenting and Communicating Findings means record commands, timestamps, and artifact locations; include a short narrative of tests and findings so others can continue the investigation or perform analysis.. In practical terms, capture your steps and artifacts for collaboration and postmortem learning. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Minimal Incident Record
  1. Time and timezone of observed symptom.
  2. Commands executed and the exact outputs saved to files.
  3. Locations of artifacts: sosreport path and /var/crash vmcore files.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will learn how senior operators approach complex RHEL incidents using disciplined methods and a small set of deep diagnostic tools. You will understand structured troubleshooting—how to observe, hypothesize, predict, test, and iterate—so that you avoid guesswork and follow a repeatable path to root cause. We will also cover three essential tools: sosreport for comprehensive environment capture, kdump for kernel crash dumps and vmcore analysis, and journalctl for focused log queries. You will see how these tools fit together with systemd debugging when services fail, and how to synthesize data from network, storage, application, and kernel layers into a coherent investigation. I will give concrete examples, such as diagnosing a failing web service that appears to be network-related but is caused by a resource limit, and highlight common misconceptions like treating logs as the only evidence or jumping to reboots before collecting dumps. By the end, you will have a practical roadmap that reduces time-to-resolution and preserves evidence for deeper analysis.

This chapter develops four verified competencies you will use daily as an RHCA. First, you will apply structured troubleshooting, including the scientific method and divide-and-conquer, to isolate complex failures across network, storage, application, and kernel layers. You will learn how disciplined observation, predictable tests, and careful iteration reduce time-to-resolution. Second, you will be able to collect and manage comprehensive diagnostic evidence with sosreport; this includes running a secure collection and understanding what to share with trusted support. Third, you will configure and test kdump so kernel panics generate vmcore files you can analyze or provide to support. Finally, you will master advanced journalctl querying and systemd unit debugging techniques to rapidly locate service failures. Each objective combines a practical skill, a reason it matters in production, and a small visual mnemonic to help you remember the workflow.

Let's unpack each objective into concrete actions you'll perform in production. For structured troubleshooting you will collect symptoms, form testable hypotheses, and run targeted commands such as ping, ss, and journalctl to validate predictions. For sosreport you will run sudo sosreport, record the generated archive path, and secure the file before sharing. For kdump you will check that the kdump service is enabled, verify crashkernel reservations in GRUB, and configure a reliable dump target like /var/crash; in VMs you will trigger a controlled panic to confirm vmcore creation. For journalctl and systemd, you will routinely use filters—unit, priority, time range, and kernel—to reduce noise, inspect unit files with systemctl cat, and verify properties with systemctl show. Each of these actions reduces uncertainty and produces artifacts you can analyze or provide to support teams.

The scientific method gives you a disciplined way to reduce uncertainty in complex incidents. Start by observing: gather symptom data such as service error messages, metrics spikes, or user reports. From those observations form a hypothesis — a concise, testable claim like "the web server is slow because the database is overloaded." Next predict what you should see if that hypothesis is true, for example increased database C P U and slow query times. Then test your prediction with focused tools: run queries, check iostat, use ss or tcpdump, and inspect journalctl entries for correlated timestamps. Analyze the results: if evidence supports the hypothesis, implement a controlled fix and verify system behavior; if not, iterate with a refined hypothesis. A common mistake is skipping evidence collection before changing configuration; that destroys the ability to reproduce or analyze. Another pitfall is testing too many variables at once. A good concrete example: if users report timeouts, hypothesize whether network, app, or storage is causing latency, then predict measurable indicators for each and test them sequentially. The core takeaway is that a tested hypothesis is more reliable than guesswork and produces artifacts you can review later.

Divide and conquer is a complementary strategy that helps you quickly eliminate whole classes of causes. When a service is unreachable or slow, start by asking which broad domain could explain the symptoms: network, storage, or application. For example, if a service port is inaccessible, test basic connectivity first with ping and tcpdump to rule out network faults. If network checks pass, verify whether storage latency is causing slow responses with iostat or LVM tools. Only after isolating the domain should you dig into application-level logs with journalctl or strace. The value of this approach is that it prevents you from chasing irrelevant signals. A practical sequence might be: ping to verify host reachability, ss or netstat to confirm listening sockets, firewall checks with firewalld status or tcpdump to see dropped packets, then systemctl status and journalctl for the service itself. Remember that domains can interact: a network partition can cause application queues to fill, which then stresses storage. Document each boundary test so you can backtrack and combine evidence later. Divide and Conquer Troubleshooting means use simple boundary tests to rule out network, storage, or application layers before deep-diving into one area.. In practical terms, narrow the domain: network, storage, or application. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

sosreport packages a wide range of system information into a single compressed archive, which is extremely useful for support cases and baselining. You run it with sudo sosreport; it may prompt for a case ID and additional notes. The generated tar. xz contains configuration files, kernel modules, network and storage information, and system logs—everything a support engineer or an experienced troubleshooter needs to understand system state. Use sosreport when you need a complete snapshot before making large changes or when opening a support case. Handle the archive carefully because it can include sensitive data such as network configuration, installed packages, and log contents. A useful practice is to inspect contents locally before sharing and to redact or transfer the file using secure channels. A common misconception is that sosreport replaces targeted log analysis; in reality it complements focused commands like journalctl by preserving a broad context that can reveal interactions across components. sosreport — Collecting a Full Diagnostic Snapshot means sosreport captures a comprehensive snapshot useful for support and baselining; treat the archive as sensitive evidence.. In practical terms, when and how to run sosreport, and why it matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

kdump is the kernel crash dumping facility that saves a memory image when the kernel panics. It reserves a portion of memory for a capture kernel; when the primary kernel fails, the machine boots a small capture kernel that writes the vmcore file to disk. That vmcore contains the system's memory image at the time of panic and is invaluable for diagnosing low-level kernel faults. To rely on kdump in production, ensure the kdump service is enabled and that you have reserved sufficient crashkernel memory in GRUB configuration, and that the dump target is a reliable storage path such as /var/crash or a network location. Testing kdump should be done only in VMs: you can trigger a panic with a safe, controlled command in a lab environment. After a reboot, verify that a vmcore file exists in /var/crash. One misconception is assuming vmcore analysis is trivial: it requires specialized tools like crash and kernel symbol knowledge. However, collecting the dump reliably is the critical first step and allows either your team or Red Hat to perform deeper analysis. kdump and vmcore — Capturing Kernel Panics means kdump preserves a vmcore image at panic time — configure, enable, and test kdump in vms so you have artifacts for kernel-level investigations.. In practical terms, how kdump works, what vmcore contains, and safe testing practices. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. journalctl is the primary log analysis tool for systemd-based systems. While basic use shows you logs, advanced filtering transforms noisy output into targeted evidence. You can filter by unit with journalctl -u service, by priority using -p err or -p warning, by time range with --since and --until, and by executable using the _COMM field. Kernel messages are accessible via -k and you can follow live logs with -f. Combining filters is powerful: for example journalctl -u httpd. service --since "yesterday" -p err returns only error messages for the httpd unit since yesterday. Use -b -1 to review the previous boot if you suspect an issue that caused a reboot. A common misconception is relying only on text searches; timestamps and priority levels are often more reliable for correlation. systemd is central to how services are started and managed in RHEL. When a unit fails, begin with sudo systemctl status to see the current state and recent log lines. Use sudo systemctl is-failed to quickly check failure, and sudo systemctl show to inspect properties such as ExecStart, Environment, Requires, and resource limits. Display the unit file with sudo systemctl cat and verify ExecStart paths, user contexts, working directories, and file permissions. Also check dependencies with sudo systemctl list-dependencies to ensure required units are active. Common configuration issues include incorrect ExecStart paths, missing dependencies, and resource limits like LimitNOFILE or LimitNPROC that are too low. In real incidents you will often need to synthesize data from multiple components to form a convincing causal chain. Begin by assembling a timeline of events using timestamps from journalctl, application logs, monitoring metrics, and tcpdump captures. Create a sequence like: network error at T0, increased application retries at T1, elevated input and output wait at T2, system panic at T3. This timeline helps you reason about causality rather than correlation. Use sosreport to capture the overall environment and vmcore to capture kernel state if a panic occurred. When correlating data, pay attention to clock skew and timezone issues so timestamps align. One common pitfall is treating a symptom as the cause because it appears first in a log; instead, ask whether the observed symptom could be downstream of another failure. These three concepts capture the practical core of advanced troubleshooting. First, structured troubleshooting—use observation, hypothesis, prediction, testing, analysis, and iteration—so your investigations are evidence-driven and reproducible. Together these ideas form a workflow: eliminate broad domains quickly, design small tests, collect artifacts before changing state, and document every step.
